chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad ibn Usman, from Al-Halby, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the shaded mosques, is it disliked to pray therein? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, but it would not harm you today, and if justice (the Qaim) had been established, you would see what would be done regarding that.'

He (the narrator) said: 'And I asked him, can a man hang weapons in the mosque? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, and as for the Great Mosque, then no, for my grandfather (peace be upon him) forbade a man trimming an arrow in the mosque.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on praying in shaded mosques and hanging weapons inside them according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the distinction between general mosques and the Masjid al-Haram regarding the storage of weapons, reflecting the practical needs of the early Muslim community while maintaining sanctity. The Imam’s mention of 'Al-Qaim' (the Awaited Imam) introduces an eschatological dimension, suggesting that the current leniency is a temporary concession that will give way to stricter enforcement of ritual purity and decorum under the era of universal justice. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on contextualizing legal maxims within both historical circumstances and future divine order.
